title: The dashboard that counted twice
outcome: A stream-processing instance restarted, some sales were counted twice, and late sales were dropped without a trace.

content.bookmark: Kafka Streams is at-least-once by default; exactly_once_v2 makes reading, updating state and writing results one transaction. Late records past a window's grace period are dropped.

check.prompt: What is Kafka Streams' default processing.guarantee?
check.why: The default is at_least_once. After a failure, some records can be processed again, so a count can go up twice.

options: Removes duplicates from the input topic
Commits the input offsets, state changes and output in one transaction, so a failure replays none of it twice
check.why: Within Kafka, the transactional producer writes output and consumer offsets atomically. It doesn't reach outside Kafka.

check.prompt: A sale arrives after its hourly window's grace period has passed. What happens?
options: It is added to the window
It goes into the next window
check.why: The grace period is how long a window waits for out-of-order records. After it, records for that window are dropped.

check.prompt: A downstream app reads the Streams output topic. What should it set to see only committed results?
check.why: read_committed hides records from aborted transactions, and those not yet committed.

caseStudy.setting: A retail chain (fictional) runs a Kafka Streams application that counts sales per store per hour from the sales topic and writes totals to sales.hourly. A dashboard used by store managers reads sales.hourly. The app runs three instances with default settings and an hourly window with a 5-minute grace period.

events.what: One instance is killed during a deployment. Its tasks move to the other instances, which restore state and continue from the last committed offsets.
Several stores' 11:00 totals on the dashboard are higher than their tills show.
Finance also finds sales from stores with poor connectivity missing entirely from Saturday's hourly totals. Those tills uploaded in batches up to 30 minutes late.

pipeline: Tills · send sales events, sometimes in late batches
sales topic · 12 partitions, so up to 12 tasks
Streams app · 3 instances, count per store per hour, grace 5 minutes, at_least_once
tasks: Why were some totals too high?

debrief.title: Why totals were too high
text: With at_least_once, an instance that dies has processed records whose offsets weren't yet committed. The task restarts from the last commit and counts them again.
exactly_once_v2 commits offsets, state updates and output together. A restart then replays nothing that was already counted.

debrief.title: Why late sales vanished
text: Windows use event time. A sale from 11:40 belongs in the 11:00 window, whatever time it arrives.
With a 5-minute grace period, the 11:00 window stopped accepting records at about 12:05 of stream time. Sales uploaded later than that were dropped.
Set the grace period from how late data really arrives, here at least 30 minutes, and accept that totals for an hour change until it closes.

debrief.title: What readers must know
text: An aggregation's output is a table that updates: a later record revises the total. The dashboard should show the latest value per store and hour, not add them up.
Readers of the output should use read_committed once exactly_once_v2 is on.

takeaway: Streams defaults to at-least-once; counts need exactly_once_v2.
Records later than the grace period are dropped.
Windowed totals are updates; read the latest value.
content.honesty: If you haven't run Kafka Streams in production, say so and explain the guarantees and windows. If you have, lead with how you chose the grace period.

tasks: What would you specify for these totals?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "Can a sale ever be counted twice or not at all?"
"How late can sales arrive, and do we still count them?"

debrief.title: Specification
text: Hourly totals match the tills once an hour is closed, including sales arriving up to an agreed lateness; tested with a restart and with late batches.

sayIt.question: How would you make sure real-time totals can be trusted?
points: Specify: every sale counted once.
Agree how late data may arrive and still count.
Show when a total is final versus still updating.
Test restarts and late data.
Reconcile against the system of record.

tasks: What do you tell store managers?
How do you set expectations for real-time numbers?

debrief.title: Store managers
text: Saturday's hourly figures were wrong for some stores; give corrected totals and the date of the fix.

debrief.title: Expectations
text: Real-time figures are provisional until late data is in. Label them on the dashboard.

sayIt.question: Users saw real-time numbers that were wrong. How do you rebuild trust?
points: Correct the numbers and say so.
Explain simply: some sales counted twice after a restart, some arrived too late.
Label provisional versus final figures.
Reconcile against the tills automatically.
Prioritise the fix.

tasks: How do you deliver the fix safely?

debrief.title: Delivering
text: Change the guarantee and grace period, reprocess Saturday from the sales topic, compare with tills, then switch the dashboard.

debrief.title: Deployments
text: Rolling restarts are normal events; test them as part of release.

sayIt.question: How would you validate a fix to a streaming calculation?
points: Reprocess the affected period from the source topic.
Compare with the system of record.
Test the failure that caused it: a restart, late data.
Switch users over once it matches.
Keep the comparison running.

debrief.title: Settings
text: processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2; grace period of at least 30 minutes; dashboard consumers with isolation.level=read_committed.

debrief.title: Scaling
text: Tasks come from input partitions: 12 partitions means up to 12 tasks spread over instances. State stores are backed by changelog topics; standby replicas cut restore time after a failure.

sayIt.question: Explain exactly-once processing and windowing in Kafka Streams.
points: Default is at_least_once; a failure can reprocess records.
exactly_once_v2 commits offsets, state and output in one transaction.
It holds inside Kafka; external systems need their own idempotency.
Windows use event time; the grace period decides how late a record can be.
Aggregations produce a table of updates; parallelism is capped by input partitions.
